question.question: On SQL Server 2022, an ordinary reporting user has no inherited data permissions and no administrative role. The user must read all columns of dbo.Contact but see unmasked values only for its masked Phone column. Schema changes are not permitted. Which two narrowly scoped permissions satisfy this requirement? Select two.

answerChoices.text: ALTER ANY MASK at database scope

question.explanation: Grant table SELECT and column-level UNMASK for Phone.
question.deepExplanation: Data access and masking presentation are separate controls. UNMASK alone grants no SELECT access, while broader administrative mask-management permissions are unnecessary and outside the stated authorization scope.

whyOtherAnswersAreWrong.b: Metadata visibility is not a substitute for SELECT or UNMASK. It does not authorize the required unmasked table-data read.
whyOtherAnswersAreWrong.d: ALTER ANY MASK manages mask definitions; it grants neither SELECT nor column-level UNMASK, so it cannot replace either required permission. Changing a mask also requires table ALTER and is outside the stated no-schema-change workflow.

claims.summary: SELECT authorizes reading the table. It is required in addition to UNMASK and does not itself reveal the masked Phone values.
Metadata visibility is not a substitute for SELECT or UNMASK. It does not authorize the required unmasked table-data read.
SQL Server 2022 supports column-scoped UNMASK. Combined with SELECT, it reveals Phone without requiring broader unmasking permission.

ALTER ANY MASK manages mask definitions; it grants neither SELECT nor column-level UNMASK, so it cannot replace either required permission. Changing a mask also requires table ALTER and is outside the stated no-schema-change workflow.

optionChallenges.claimRepresented: Table-level SELECT authorizes this reporting user to read every column of dbo.Contact; it does not itself remove dynamic masks.
optionChallenges.whyIncorrectInContext: NOT incorrect in the intended permission set: a supplies the read access that c cannot provide. SELECT alone still returns masked Phone values. Sufficiency assumes no conflicting permissions and no separate effective unmasking rights on other masked columns.
optionChallenges.couldBeCorrectWhen: It is required together with c for the intended ordinary reporting principal. SELECT alone is also appropriate when a reader should receive masked values for every masked column; the saved example demonstrates that separate scenario.
optionChallenges.evidenceSummary: dp800-d2-masking, Permissions, decoded lines 43-55, explicitly separates table SELECT from UNMASK. The SELECT-only demonstration at lines 166-187 returns masked values. Neither passage requires broad db_datareader membership for a table-scoped grant.

optionChallenges.claimRepresented: VIEW DEFINITION on dbo.Contact is offered as a competing permission for the required table-data read and Phone-only unmasking.
optionChallenges.whyIncorrectInContext: It is not a replacement for the SELECT and UNMASK requirements under the intended reading. However, the sole admitted receipt never names VIEW DEFINITION. Its exact semantics and the asserted metadata-only exclusion are not independently established merely by the linked article title.
optionChallenges.couldBeCorrectWhen: A task limited to inspecting the definition or metadata of dbo.Contact, rather than reading its rows, is the meaningful proposed alternate. The saved source separates metadata visibility from UNMASK and links Metadata Visibility Configuration, but does not document this named grant. That alternate remains unverified in this frozen citation set; I will not fabricate a sourced counterexample.
optionChallenges.evidenceSummary: dp800-d2-masking, decoded lines 45-55, supports SELECT plus UNMASK and distinguishes metadata visibility. It contains no VIEW DEFINITION occurrence. https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/sql/relational-databases/security/metadata-visibility-configuration is only a reference in the receipt, not independently fetched content admitted for this item. This is an evidence gap, not a claim that b is the correct answer.

optionChallenges.claimRepresented: SQL Server 2022 column-level UNMASK for dbo.Contact.Phone reveals that masked column without granting UNMASK on every masked column.
optionChallenges.whyIncorrectInContext: NOT incorrect under the intended effective-permission baseline: SQL Server 2022 supports column scope, and a provides the separate SELECT permission. A new narrow grant does not establish Phone-only effective rights if another direct UNMASK grant already exists; the stem does not explicitly close that starting-state possibility.
optionChallenges.couldBeCorrectWhen: It is valid for a SQL Server 2022 principal whose effective read access is supplied by a and whose other masked columns lack UNMASK or overriding authority. The documentation first supplies reading permission before demonstrating column UNMASK; selecting c alone would not supply data access.
optionChallenges.evidenceSummary: dp800-d2-masking, decoded lines 123-125, explicitly introduces column-level UNMASK in SQL Server 2022. Lines 304-319 separately supply db_datareader access and then grant UNMASK on one named column; a is the narrower table-read substitute in this question. Lines 45-55 establish the independent SELECT prerequisite.

optionChallenges.claimRepresented: Database-scoped ALTER ANY MASK grants authority relevant to administering mask definitions, rather than the requested read and selective-unmask permissions.
optionChallenges.whyIncorrectInContext: It supplies neither of the two required read-path permissions and is broader than the named table and column need. Granting d is not itself a schema change. Using it to add, replace or remove a mask additionally requires table ALTER and would violate the no-schema-change workflow; that is distinct from merely granting the permission.
optionChallenges.couldBeCorrectWhen: A security officer authorized to add, replace or remove masks on an existing table can appropriately receive ALTER ANY MASK together with ALTER on that table. Schema modification must be permitted in that alternate administration scenario. The permission is useful there without making it a SELECT or UNMASK substitute here.
optionChallenges.evidenceSummary: dp800-d2-masking, decoded lines 47-51, distinguishes CONTROL, UNMASK and ALTER ANY MASK and explicitly names both mask-modification prerequisites and the security-officer use case. Lines 90 and 191-205 corroborate actual schema-changing mask operations. The repaired d explanation no longer confuses permission with operation.

challenges.scope: On the intended effective-permission reading, table SELECT plus Phone-column UNMASK is appropriately scoped. Other already-masked columns remain masked only absent other effective UNMASK or overriding authority. This concerns ordinary query-result presentation, not cryptographic secrecy or prevention of inference. dp800-d2-masking, decoded lines 16-23, 45-55, 100-125.
challenges.plan: Enumerated all six proposed self-sufficient pairs: a+c supplies both controls; a+b lacks Phone UNMASK; a+d lacks UNMASK and cannot lawfully remove a mask; b+c lacks SELECT; b+d lacks both read controls; c+d lacks SELECT. No second self-sufficient pair is supported. Different incremental-grant answers become possible only by importing unspecified pre-existing direct rights, which is why the starting-state wording matters.
challenges.role: The stem excludes inherited data permissions and administrative roles, not all existing direct permissions. A reporting principal could already hold direct SELECT or direct UNMASK on another masked column without an administrative role. Direct overriding authority also is not equivalent to role membership. The source makes effective CONTROL and UNMASK decisive, not job title alone; the unconditional Phone-only outcome is under-specified. dp800-d2-masking, decoded lines 45-55 and 77.
challenges.preconditions: SQL Server 2022 and an existing masked Phone column are explicit. The proposal additionally assumes an ordinary permitted grantor, no effective denial defeating the read, and no existing direct UNMASK on other masked columns. Grantor creation or execution is not the task, so I do not demand login-creation options; the unresolved effective-permission baseline is the material gap. The article requires SELECT alongside UNMASK and distinguishes overriding CONTROL at decoded lines 45-55.
challenges.featureStatus: The frozen product receipt expressly supports SQL Server 2022 column UNMASK at decoded lines 123-125 and demonstrates it at lines 318-319. The recorded GA status is consistent with the documented released-version feature. I make no fresh-live availability claim and do not import Azure service tiers, Fabric workspace roles or Fabric EXECUTE AS restrictions into this SQL Server question.

challenges.stemSufficiency: The stem is sufficient to infer the intended a+c permission set but not to attest every possible starting state it literally permits. No inherited permissions is narrower than no existing direct or inherited effective permissions. Phone-only should also be read as only among already-masked columns, not as automatically masking otherwise unmasked columns. These qualifications must not be silently supplied to obtain an unconditional pass.
challenges.explanationBounds: The repair to d is sound: a permission grant alone does not change schema, and mask modification requires ALTER ANY MASK plus table ALTER. The explanation correctly separates SELECT and UNMASK. The b rationale still lacks named-permission evidence in the admitted receipt. Do not expand the item into a guarantee against inference; the product security note expressly disclaims that protection at decoded lines 100-119.
challenges.reasoningDepth: The item combines data access with column-level presentation control, but the answer is a short two-permission recipe. It presents no effective-grant inventory, conflicting permission, result set, code diagnosis or implementation trade-off to resolve. SQL Server 2022 scope is useful, yet the advanced label is not convincingly earned by this construction.
challenges.answerClues: The correct permission names closely echo read and unmasked in the stem. VIEW DEFINITION looks like metadata, while database-scope ALTER ANY MASK contrasts with narrowly scoped and the no-schema-change constraint. Declaring Select two is appropriate, not itself a defect; the weakness is that semantic elimination substantially substitutes for advanced reasoning.
